review.headline: A wild tactical skirmish ends in a direct king hunt

sections.text: Black chose an awkward setup with 5...Bd6?, blocking their own d-pawn. You developed naturally with 6.O-O and created tension with 7.Bg5, setting up a pin along the d8-h4 diagonal. After trades in the center, Black slipped with 10...d6??, allowing you to trap their bishop with 11.f4!.
The game quickly turned chaotic. After 12...g5, you played 13.Bxg5?? instead of taking the knight on f6, and after 14.Rf2? Nxe4? 15.Re2?? Bg4, Black took an exchange and held the upper hand at -3.4.

Black failed to consolidate and played 18...Re8?, allowing you to launch an attack with 19.Qh5!, setting up a pin on the f7-pawn. Black's defensive try 19...Qf6?? backfired against 20.Rf1! Qg7, letting you break through with the fork 21.Bxf7+! and quickly deliver mate.

review.headline: A wild queenside clash ends in a backfire

sections.text: The game opened quietly, but the queenside pawn structure soon created serious tactical tension. White pushed forward with 7.c5 and 8.b4, and both sides spent the next several moves missing key pawn breaks. You allowed 14.bxc6, where the pawn landed with a fork on your bishop and knight. White gave the advantage right back with 15.Ne5, and your 15...Nxe5! was the correct response, trading off the attacker and letting you snap up a pawn with 16...Qxe5.

With an extra pawn and an active queen, you had control, but you let White back into the game by avoiding a trade. When White offered queens with 17.Qc3, retreating with 17...Qc7?? gave away your edge. Snatching another pawn with 18...Bxa4?? left your pieces uncoordinated, and White struck with 19.c6, unleashing a discovered attack from the bishop on a3 against your bishop on e7. Rather than eliminating that bishop with 19...Bxa3, your 19...Rfc8?? dropped a piece to 20.Bxe7.

Despite losing material, you still had chances to fight if you stayed alert to White's dangerous passed pawn. Instead, catastrophe struck on move 25. White blundered with 25.Bxb5??, leaving the c7-pawn undefended. But rather than playing 25...Rxc7, you captured with 25...axb5??. That opened the a-file, allowing 26.Rxa8 Rxa8 27.c8=Q+, completely collapsing your position.

review.turning_point: The critical mistake was 25...axb5??, which ignored White's dangerous passed pawn on c7. Capturing the bishop immediately cost you a rook on a8 and allowed White to queen.
review.focus: Always evaluate checks and captures before grabbing loose material; on 25...axb5??, removing the passed pawn with 25...Rxc7 was essential.
